Lord Ye's Love of Dragons: Do You Love a Real Being, or an Image That Cannot Answer Back?
Hearing that Duke Ai of Lu loved worthy scholars, Zizhang traveled a thousand li to visit him.
He waited seven days without receiving the courtesy he was due.
Before leaving, Zizhang asked someone to pass a story on to the duke.
Lord Ye loved dragons.

Clothing hooks, utensils, carvings, and pictures throughout his house all bore their images. Hearing that such a dragon-lover existed, a real dragon descended from the sky, put its head through the window, and trailed its tail into the hall.
At the sight, Lord Ye turned and ran, utterly distraught.
Zizhang said:

Lord Ye did not love dragons. He loved things that resembled dragons but were not real dragons. What you love, likewise, is not the scholar who actually comes before you, but a reputation for “loving scholars” that takes up none of your time and requires no response.
“Lord Ye's love of dragons” later became a phrase for someone who professes to love something but retreats in fear when actually confronted with it.
But calling Lord Ye inconsistent does not finish reading the story.
What, exactly, distinguishes a real dragon from one painted on a wall?
The most obvious difference is danger.
Anyone might be frightened by a real dragon putting its head through a window.

A painted dragon will not suddenly move or turn a house into an unpredictable space. Lord Ye's flight at the sight of a real dragon cannot, simply through fear, prove that every earlier affection was false.
Someone can love the sea and fear a storm.
Loving wild animals does not mean wanting one in the bedroom.
Loving power, speed, or the unknown does not mean abandoning judgment about real risks.
If the fable means only “If you really love it, you shouldn't be afraid,” it becomes a dangerous demand:
Prove your feelings are real by accepting every consequence.
But the complete story places the dragon fable within the relationship between Zizhang and Duke Ai, limiting that interpretation.
Zizhang is not an uncontrollable wild beast.
He comes because Duke Ai has established a reputation for “loving scholars.” The duke need not accept all his advice, give him a position, or assume that he is necessarily worthy and capable.
At least, however, he needs to allow this actual person to be met and considered.
Instead, he offers not even basic courtesy.
This shifts the story's focus from “being frightened of a dangerous object” to something else:
**If you love an ideal image, are you willing to bear the cost of meeting its real counterpart?**
The painted dragon has many advantages.
It always appears in the pose Lord Ye chooses.
He arranges its size, position, and color. It cannot move, correct his idea of dragons, or demand that the house make new room for it.
He can admire it whenever he likes, and turn away whenever he likes.
The image gives him a sense of “being close to dragons” without letting another being actually enter his life.
A real dragon is different.
Once it arrives, Lord Ye is no longer the only party deciding how the encounter will unfold.

The dragon has a body, direction, and actions of its own. It may come too close or bring consequences Lord Ye has not prepared for. Even if it comes in goodwill after hearing of his love of dragons, he must face a response he cannot entirely arrange.
This is also one of the most fundamental differences between actual people and our ideals of people.
We can like “people who know their own minds.”
But someone who really knows their own mind will disagree with us at important moments.
We can admire “candor.”
But actual candor does not necessarily say only what we want to hear.
We can praise “independence.”
But a truly independent person may take their life in a direction we disapprove of.
We can say we value “diversity.”
But once differences affect shared arrangements, rather than merely provide decorative colors, they ask us to relinquish some control.
It is easy to like these words.
Meeting them in reality means meeting a person whose story we do not get to finish writing.
That does not mean we must accept everything whenever someone contradicts us, causes trouble, or makes demands.
Reality is no guarantee of legitimacy.

A real dragon can be dangerous, and a real person can harm, deceive, or cross boundaries. Recognizing that another is not an image we invented does not mean giving up our judgment or ability to refuse.
Lord Ye can certainly shut the door.
Duke Ai can also meet Zizhang and decide that his advice is unsuitable.
The story criticizes not a final refusal, but professing to love a kind of being while denying its actual representatives any place to be seen and judged.
If “I love worthy scholars” means only liking words about scholars on the wall, it undertakes no real relationship.
An actual scholar arriving before a ruler takes time, offers judgments, and may force the ruler to face questions he would rather avoid.
If affection withdraws before any of this begins, what it loves may be only the image the ideal gives its owner:
I am someone who loves dragons.
I am someone who values talent.
I am someone who welcomes disagreement.
These are pleasing identities, and none requires the object actually to appear.
Lord Ye's house, then, is not merely overdecorated.
It resembles a world under his complete control.
Dragons are everywhere, yet not one can change anything.
This is the great convenience of images.
We can adorn ourselves with an image of a group, a profession, a way of life, or a virtue without entering real relationships with the particular people who belong to it.
Liking “the resilience of the poor” does not mean being willing to hear a poor person explain how institutions constrain them.
Praising “the dedication of caregivers” does not mean allowing a caregiver to say they cannot go on.
Admiring “young people's creativity” does not mean giving them room to decide when they propose a different approach.
Respecting “tradition” does not mean facing the differences and disputes that actually exist within it.
The image is always tidier.
It selects the parts we want to admire and leaves outside the frame the parts that answer back, refuse, or demand a new understanding.
Someone may therefore truly love an image and sincerely be moved by it, without ever having loved an actual being.
The “falseness” here need not be a deliberate lie.
Lord Ye may never have realized that what he liked was a dragon arranged by himself.
Only when the real dragon appears do the conditions of his affection become visible for the first time.
This is why an actual encounter often tests us more than an ideal does.
Before the object appears, principles are easy to declare.
Once it arrives, those principles begin to require something of us:
Giving others time.
Letting our judgments receive a response.
Acknowledging that the object does not match our imagination.
Changing arrangements when necessary.
Or at least explaining why we still refuse in the end.
This does not require every encounter to become a close relationship.
Some relationships can only remain distant, some opinions will not be adopted, and some conflicts cannot be resolved.
But if we describe ourselves through a form of love, respect, or welcome, we must accept that actual people or things have a chance to make that description less comfortable.
Otherwise, what we like is merely a word that will never examine us.
Lord Ye's fear reveals something else.
The real object may not only differ from the ideal, but exceed the scale we can bear.
Someone who says they seek the truth may, on encountering facts that would destroy their existing plans, discover that they are not ready.
A group that says it welcomes dissent may feel threatened when actual dissent unsettles its central arrangements.
A parent who wants a child to become themselves may discover the distance between liking independence and bearing it when the child actually chooses a different life.
At such moments, fear does not necessarily mean everything said before was false.
It may mean our abilities have not yet caught up with our principles.
What matters is what we do next.
We can acknowledge:
I really was not ready.
I need to set safety boundaries.
My original understanding was too simple.
All these answers are more honest than pretending the actual object “doesn't count as a real dragon.”
If Lord Ye merely steps back in fear, the story can continue.
The real question is whether he will reconsider his love, or preserve his identity as a “dragon-lover” by continuing to paint only dragons that never come before him.
Zizhang sent this story to Duke Ai because he needed to identify not an aesthetic preference, but a false openness in power.
Someone with decision-making authority can easily praise talent.
Praise changes none of their arrangements.
Once actual talent arrives, however, it may require a meeting, raise objections, influence policy, or at least require the ruler to judge personally rather than merely enjoy a reputation.
If “loving scholars” only adorns the ruler while actual scholars never enter the process of judgment, they are like the dragons on the wall:
The more there are, the more they demonstrate the owner's taste.
Yet not one can truly change the owner.
This is the story's deepest edge.
It does not merely mock personal hypocrisy. It examines whether a power that professes to welcome outside opinions actually lets them come to its window.
“Lord Ye's love of dragons” need not therefore be reduced to:
Do not pretend to like what you fear.
The more precise question is:
Do I like an image that I define, display, and know will never interrupt me, or am I willing to let the real thing appear in a way I do not entirely control?
The first kind of liking may still be real.
People can sincerely love painted dragons, heroes in books, imagined freedom, and abstract justice.
But that love alone does not entitle us to declare ourselves ready to respond to actual dragons, heroes, freedom, or justice.
Images move us.
Reality asks us to act, judge, and take responsibility.
The distance between the two is not crossed naturally in a single step.
Only when the real dragon reached the window did Lord Ye discover that his love had a condition:
The dragons must remain merely the dragons in his house.
A real being, by contrast, never promises to appear only in a form we find convenient to bear.

*Textual basis: the account of Zizhang's visit to Duke Ai of Lu preserved in the New Prefaces, “Miscellaneous Matters V.” Hearing that the duke loved scholars, Zizhang traveled a great distance to meet him, received no proper courtesy for seven days, and used Lord Ye's love of dragons as an analogy upon leaving. This essay uses that full frame rather than only the later independent idiom. Its focus is therefore not fear at the sight of a real dragon itself, but the difference between liking a controllable ideal image and responding to a particular visitor in reality.*
